courseDetails.title: Introduction to News Writing
courseDetails.description: A 100-level Mass Communication course covering the meaning and functions of news, news values, newsroom roles, ethical reporting, news gathering, source evaluation, story structure, specialised reporting, editing, media law, digital journalism, and multimedia distribution.

questions.question: Which description best defines news?
options: A fictional account written mainly for entertainment
Any private message exchanged between two people
Relevant information about recent events or developments of public interest
A paid message promoting a product or service
questions.explanation: News concerns recent or newly significant events that are relevant to a substantial part of the public.

questions.question: Which news value is strongest when an event has just occurred?
options: Proximity
Prominence
Human interest
Timeliness
questions.explanation: Timeliness refers to recency. The more current an event is, the greater its usual news value.

questions.question: A fire occurring in a reader’s neighbourhood is likely to receive attention mainly because of which news value?
options: Unusualness
Proximity
Prominence
Conflict
questions.explanation: Proximity increases interest because audiences tend to care more about events that occur near them geographically or emotionally.

questions.question: A new policy affects every public university student in the country. Which news value is most evident?
options: Novelty
Impact
Proximity
Entertainment
questions.explanation: Impact measures how many people an event affects and how significantly it affects them.

questions.question: A dispute between two political parties is especially newsworthy because it contains what?
options: Continuity
Advertising
Conflict
Routine
questions.explanation: Disagreements and clashes create conflict, a recognised news value that often attracts audience attention.

questions.question: Why would the resignation of a famous governor attract substantial news coverage?
options: It is necessarily humorous
It is always local to every audience
It involves a prominent person
It contains no public consequence
questions.explanation: Prominence makes the actions of famous or influential individuals more newsworthy.

questions.question: A goat being elected honorary mayor of a small town would mainly demonstrate which news value?
options: Continuity
Objectivity
Unusualness
Attribution
questions.explanation: Unusual or unexpected events stand out from ordinary experience and therefore attract coverage.

questions.question: A story about a child rescuing neighbours during a flood relies strongly on which news value?
options: Defamation
Embargo
Convergence
Human interest
questions.explanation: Human-interest stories evoke emotion by focusing on personal courage, suffering, achievement, or survival.

questions.question: Which activity best illustrates the watchdog function of news?
options: Publishing only official celebrations
Repeating advertisements during a bulletin
Investigating and exposing misuse of public funds
Avoiding questions about powerful institutions
questions.explanation: The watchdog role holds authorities and powerful institutions accountable through scrutiny and investigation.

questions.question: When a report explains the scientific background of an epidemic, news is performing which function?
options: Entertaining advertisers
Educating the public
Protecting sources from all questions
Replacing public debate
questions.explanation: News educates when it provides context and explanations that help audiences understand complex issues.

questions.question: During an approaching storm, a station broadcasts evacuation routes and safety instructions. Which function of news is most evident?
options: Product placement
Crisis communication
Celebrity promotion
Literary criticism
questions.explanation: During emergencies, news can quickly provide life-saving information and coordinate public response.

questions.question: How does news serve as a historical record?
options: It predicts every future event accurately
It removes all disagreement from society
It documents events that can later be studied in archives
It prevents reports from being updated
questions.explanation: Published reports and broadcasts preserve documented accounts of past events and developments.

questions.question: Which subject is most typical of hard news?
options: A profile of a popular musician
A guide to weekend fashion
A reflective travel story
An urgent report on a new national budget
questions.explanation: Hard news covers serious, timely, and consequential subjects such as politics, crime, economics, and emergencies.

questions.question: Which description best fits soft news?
options: Live reporting of a major earthquake
A factual alert about a national emergency
An immediate court judgment affecting millions
Less urgent content focused on lifestyle, entertainment, or human interest
questions.explanation: Soft news is generally less formal and less urgent, often using a feature-oriented or personal approach.

questions.question: What most clearly distinguishes investigative news?
options: It reports only sporting results
It avoids documents and interviews
It uses extensive research to uncover hidden wrongdoing or suppressed facts
It is always published as a short social-media caption
questions.explanation: Investigative journalism goes beyond routine reporting to reveal important information, often about corruption or injustice.

questions.question: What is breaking news?
options: Urgent reporting of an important event as it unfolds
A story published every year without changes
A paid announcement from an advertiser
A long historical essay with no recent development
questions.explanation: Breaking news provides real-time or near-real-time updates about urgent events of high public interest.

questions.question: Which item is an example of opinion news?
options: A verified emergency alert
An editorial interpreting a government decision
A straight report of election totals
A weather observation from an official station
questions.explanation: Editorials, commentaries, and opinion columns analyse or interpret events from an identified viewpoint.

questions.question: What is a reporter’s central role in a newsroom?
options: Approving every advertisement personally
Designing all printing machines
Gathering, verifying, and communicating newsworthy information
Representing one political party in every story
questions.explanation: Reporters find information, verify it, interview sources, and turn it into accurate news for the public.

questions.question: Why must reporters manage their time effectively?
options: They should avoid filing stories promptly
They work under deadlines while gathering and verifying information
They are expected to write only when no event is occurring
Time management replaces the need for accuracy
questions.explanation: Reporting combines interviews, research, writing, and verification under strict publication or broadcast deadlines.

questions.question: Which action demonstrates impartiality by a reporter?
options: Presenting relevant viewpoints fairly and allowing the audience to assess them
Supporting a preferred side without disclosure
Removing facts that weaken the reporter’s opinion
Using insults against one source
questions.explanation: Impartial reporting avoids taking sides and represents relevant perspectives accurately.

questions.question: Why is transparency important in reporting?
options: It permits reporters to invent anonymous quotations
It guarantees that every source is correct
It removes the need to correct mistakes
It helps audiences understand how information was obtained and what limitations exist
questions.explanation: Transparency supports trust by clarifying sources, methods, uncertainty, and possible limitations.

questions.question: A reporter receives an important claim from one person. What is the most responsible next step?
options: Publish the claim as established fact immediately
Delete the source’s name and stop checking
Seek corroboration from reliable evidence or additional sources
Add dramatic details to make it stronger
questions.explanation: Corroboration reduces the risk of publishing a false or misleading single-source claim.

questions.question: What is the purpose of a newsroom editor?
options: To prevent all reporters from using sources
To improve accuracy, clarity, structure, and compliance with publication standards
To convert every news story into an advertisement
To replace factual reporting with personal opinion
questions.explanation: Editors review and refine stories, verify key details, and ensure they meet ethical and house-style requirements.

questions.question: What does a news editor commonly consider when selecting stories?
options: News value, audience relevance, available space or time, and public importance
Only the reporter’s personal preference
The number of adjectives in each story
Whether every story praises an institution
questions.explanation: News selection involves editorial judgement about significance, timeliness, relevance, and practical constraints.

questions.question: How can reporters influence public perception?
options: The facts, voices, context, and framing they select affect how issues are understood
They have no influence once a story is published
Only advertisements shape audience understanding
Perception depends entirely on headline font size
questions.explanation: Journalistic choices about emphasis and context can shape what audiences notice and how they interpret events.

questions.question: What is a journalist’s primary ethical duty?
options: To maximise controversy regardless of facts
To protect every institution from criticism
To support private interests without disclosure
To report the truth as accurately as possible
questions.explanation: Truth and accuracy are foundational duties because public trust depends on reliable information.

questions.question: Why is journalistic independence important?
options: It allows journalists to refuse all evidence
It requires reporters to work without editors
It helps reporters avoid improper influence and conflicts of interest
It makes corrections unnecessary
questions.explanation: Independence enables journalists to serve the public rather than hidden political, financial, or personal interests.

questions.question: Which action best demonstrates accountability?
options: Silently leaving a known error online
Blaming the audience for the mistake
Deleting the entire archive to hide the error
Promptly correcting a significant factual error and explaining the correction
questions.explanation: Accountability requires journalists to take responsibility for their work and correct errors openly.

questions.question: What does the ethical principle of minimising harm require?
options: Suppressing every uncomfortable fact
Naming vulnerable victims in all circumstances
Publishing allegations before verification
Considering avoidable damage while still reporting information of legitimate public interest
questions.explanation: Journalists should balance the public need for information against unnecessary harm to individuals and communities.

questions.question: Why may a journalist withhold the identity of a sexual-assault survivor?
options: To protect the survivor’s privacy and reduce further harm
To make the report less accurate
Because names are never allowed in journalism
To prevent authorities from investigating
questions.explanation: Protecting vulnerable people is a common application of the duty to minimise harm.

questions.question: Which sentence is the most objective?
options: The careless authorities finally reopened the terrible road.
Everyone knows the officials handled the incident badly.
The obviously dishonest officers delayed traffic for no reason.
Police said the road was reopened at 6 p.m. after investigators left the scene.
questions.explanation: The objective sentence attributes a verifiable statement without adding the writer’s judgement.

questions.question: Which revision is the clearest and most concise?
options: The project was, on the day that was Monday, approved by the council members.
On Monday, it was the council that was responsible for the approval of the project in question.
The council approved the project on Monday.
The council, which is the body concerned, gave an approval regarding the said project on Monday.
questions.explanation: Clear news writing uses direct language and removes unnecessary words.

questions.question: Why should journalists avoid jargon when writing for a general audience?
options: Jargon always makes a report legally unsafe
Readers prefer sentences they cannot interpret
Jargon automatically creates objectivity
Unexplained specialist terms can make the story difficult to understand
questions.explanation: Journalists should translate technical language into accessible terms without distorting meaning.

questions.question: A reporter writes that a proposal is “ridiculous” without attributing the word to a source. What is the main problem?
options: The sentence uses too few words
The proposal is necessarily confidential
The reporter has inserted personal judgement into a news report
The statement is a secondary source
questions.explanation: Unattributed evaluative language can reveal bias and undermine objectivity.

questions.question: What is the best way to improve the accuracy of a statistic in a story?
options: Check it against the original reliable source and confirm its context
Round it upward to create impact
Use it without naming where it came from
Replace it with an estimate from memory
questions.explanation: Accuracy requires checking figures against authoritative evidence and ensuring they are not presented out of context.

questions.question: What is a structured interview?
options: An interview that follows a planned sequence of standard questions
A completely spontaneous conversation with no preparation
An observation conducted without speaking
A review of previously published articles only
questions.explanation: Structured interviews use a formal, consistent question order and are useful when comparability is important.

questions.question: What is the main advantage of an unstructured interview?
options: It guarantees every answer is brief
It prevents follow-up questions
It removes the need for active listening
It allows a flexible, free-flowing exploration of the subject
questions.explanation: Unstructured interviews permit the discussion to develop naturally and can reveal unexpected insights.

questions.question: How does a semi-structured interview work?
options: It consists entirely of yes-or-no questions
It is conducted without a topic
It combines prepared questions with flexible follow-up questions
It uses only questions submitted by advertisers
questions.explanation: Semi-structured interviews provide direction while allowing the reporter to pursue important new information.

questions.question: Why should a journalist research an interviewee before the interview?
options: To ask informed questions and avoid wasting time on easily available facts
To decide the answers the interviewee must give
To remove the need to listen during the interview
To guarantee the interviewee agrees with the reporter
questions.explanation: Preparation improves question quality and helps the journalist recognise significant or inconsistent answers.

questions.question: Which question is most likely to produce a detailed answer?
options: What challenges did you face while implementing the policy?
Did you implement the policy?
Was the meeting good?
Can you answer yes or no?
questions.explanation: Open-ended questions invite explanation, examples, and detail rather than a one-word response.

questions.question: Why is active listening essential during an interview?
options: It allows the reporter to ignore unexpected information
It helps the reporter understand answers and ask meaningful follow-ups
It eliminates the need to take notes
It ensures all questions remain identical
questions.explanation: Active listening helps the reporter notice important details, contradictions, and opportunities for clarification.

questions.question: What should a journalist do when an interviewee gives an unclear answer?
options: Rewrite the answer as the journalist prefers
Assume the intended meaning
Publish the ambiguity as a verified fact
Ask a polite clarifying follow-up question
questions.explanation: Clarification reduces misunderstanding and improves the accuracy of quotations and paraphrases.

questions.question: What is non-participant observation?
options: The journalist joins the group as an active member
The journalist observes events without becoming directly involved
The journalist publishes before arriving
The journalist gathers only anonymous opinions online
questions.explanation: Non-participant observation preserves distance while allowing the reporter to witness behaviour and events.

questions.question: What is a major strength of observation in news gathering?
options: It automatically reveals every hidden motive
It makes corroboration unnecessary
It provides direct details about actions, surroundings, and atmosphere
It guarantees the journalist has no bias
questions.explanation: Firsthand observation can make a report vivid and authentic by capturing details that sources may overlook.

questions.question: What is a common limitation of observation?
options: It can never provide sensory detail
The reporter may misinterpret what is seen because of limited context or bias
It always takes less time than every other method
It produces only secondary information
questions.explanation: Observation is selective and may not explain causes, motives, or events outside the journalist’s view.

questions.question: Which item is a primary source?
options: An eyewitness interviewed about an accident
A textbook analysing road safety
A documentary summarising earlier reports
A newspaper column interpreting the accident
questions.explanation: An eyewitness gives a direct, firsthand account of the event.

questions.question: Which item is a secondary source?
options: An official election result sheet
A scholarly article analysing previously collected election data
A candidate’s live speech
A reporter’s direct observation at a polling station
questions.explanation: Secondary sources interpret, explain, or analyse information that originated elsewhere.

questions.question: What is source verification?
options: Checking a source’s identity, knowledge, reliability, and supporting evidence
Accepting every statement because it is confident
Hiding the source from editors
Changing a source’s words to improve the story
questions.explanation: Verification helps determine whether the source is genuine, informed, consistent, and supported by evidence.

questions.question: What is the best reason to protect a confidential source?
options: Disclosure could expose the source to serious harm for providing important information
The source wants to avoid all factual checking
Anonymous claims are automatically true
The reporter wants to make the story mysterious
questions.explanation: Confidentiality may be justified when a credible source faces genuine risk and the information serves the public interest.

questions.question: What is the inverted pyramid structure?
options: An arrangement that presents the most important facts first and less important details later
A structure that hides the main point until the final paragraph
A method that orders all events alphabetically
A feature technique based only on dialogue
questions.explanation: The inverted pyramid ranks information in descending order of importance.

questions.question: Why did the telegraph contribute to the development of the inverted pyramid?
options: Reporters placed crucial facts first in case transmission was interrupted
Telegraph messages allowed unlimited detail at no cost
The telegraph was mainly used to transmit photographs
Editors could not shorten telegraph reports
questions.explanation: Early telegraph transmission could fail or be cut, so essential information had to be sent first.

questions.question: What is the lead or lede of a news story?
options: The opening paragraph containing the most important information
The final correction printed after publication
The list of every source’s telephone number
A caption placed beneath a photograph
questions.explanation: The lead gives readers the core of the story immediately.

questions.question: Which set contains the 5Ws and H?
options: Who, which, whose, whether, while, and however
Who, what, where, when, why, and how
What, width, weight, word, work, and headline
Where, write, wrong, world, web, and history
questions.explanation: These questions identify the essential facts a news lead may need to address.

questions.question: Which description best fits a summary lead?
options: An opening that delays the main fact for several pages
A concise opening that presents the central facts of a hard-news event
A list of unrelated quotations
A final paragraph offering the writer’s opinion
questions.explanation: Summary leads quickly communicate the most important 5Ws and H, particularly in hard news.

questions.question: Which opening is most characteristic of a feature lead?
options: A raw list of statistics without context
A legal disclaimer before any information
A complete bibliography in the first paragraph
A descriptive scene that draws the reader into a human-interest story
questions.explanation: Feature leads may build mood, introduce a character, or tell an anecdote before explaining the central point.

questions.question: What is the main purpose of a news headline?
options: To exaggerate details that are not in the story
To include every background fact
To summarise the story’s central point clearly and attract appropriate attention
To conceal the subject until the final paragraph
questions.explanation: A good headline is concise, accurate, specific, and faithful to the story.

questions.question: Which headline is the strongest for a straight-news report?
options: You Will Not Believe What the Council Did!
A Very Interesting Thing Happened Yesterday
Community Matters and Other Things
Council Approves New Community Health Centre
questions.explanation: The strong headline uses an active verb and states the central development clearly without sensationalism.

questions.question: Why are strong verbs useful in headlines?
options: They allow unsupported opinions to appear factual
They make the action clear and keep the headline concise
They remove the need for a story body
They make all events sound humorous
questions.explanation: Strong active verbs communicate the main action quickly and directly.

questions.question: What belongs in the body of a news story?
options: Only the reporter’s personal beliefs
Supporting facts, quotations, attribution, context, and background
The publication’s entire history
Unrelated details arranged randomly
questions.explanation: The body expands and supports the information introduced in the lead.

questions.question: Why are quotations used in a news story?
options: They allow the reporter to avoid verification
They should replace every factual sentence
They make attribution unnecessary
They provide authentic voices, evidence, and a human dimension
questions.explanation: Relevant quotations can add credibility, emotion, expertise, or firsthand perspective when accurately attributed.

questions.question: What is attribution?
options: Identifying the source of information, a claim, or a quotation
Removing all names from the story
Converting a quotation into the reporter’s opinion
Placing the least important fact first
questions.explanation: Attribution tells readers who supplied the information and helps them assess its credibility.

questions.question: Why can editors trim an inverted-pyramid story from the bottom?
options: The bottom always contains false information
The lead is repeated word for word in every paragraph
The least essential information is normally placed near the end
Headlines contain every minor detail
questions.explanation: Descending importance allows less important material to be removed without destroying the core story.

questions.question: How do news stories commonly end?
options: With a compulsory essay-style restatement of every point
With a less important detail, a relevant quotation, or a forward-looking statement
With the reporter declaring which side is correct
With the lead copied exactly
questions.explanation: Straight news usually does not require a formal argumentative conclusion; the final paragraph may offer closure or future direction.

questions.question: Which sequence best reflects a typical straight-news structure?
options: Conclusion, bibliography, title page, and abstract
Minor detail, opinion, headline, and lead
Headline, lead, body in descending importance, and less essential closing material
Quotation list, advertisement, lead, and index
questions.explanation: This sequence reflects the headline and inverted-pyramid organisation used in straight news.

questions.question: What is beat reporting?
options: Reporting any topic once without preparation
Writing only anonymous opinion columns
Repeating stories from another outlet
Consistent coverage of a particular subject area or institution
questions.explanation: A beat is an assigned area such as politics, health, education, crime, sports, or business.

questions.question: What is a major benefit of specialising in a beat?
options: The reporter no longer needs objectivity
All sources become automatically trustworthy
The reporter develops subject knowledge and reliable contacts over time
The reporter can ignore developments outside office hours
questions.explanation: Specialisation improves depth, context, source access, and the ability to identify meaningful developments.

questions.question: Which topic belongs most directly to the political beat?
options: A league football final
A clinical trial of a new vaccine
A review of a music album
A parliamentary debate on electoral reform
questions.explanation: Political reporters cover government, elections, parties, public policy, and political institutions.

questions.question: What is a key responsibility of a crime reporter?
options: Report accurately while respecting legal processes and the rights of suspects and victims
Declare every suspect guilty before trial
Publish rumours from any police contact
Reveal vulnerable victims’ identities automatically
questions.explanation: Crime reporting requires careful sourcing, legal awareness, fairness, and sensitivity.

questions.question: What should a business reporter do with complex financial terminology?
options: Repeat the jargon without explanation
Replace the figures with personal opinion
Remove all economic context
Explain it in accurate, accessible language for the intended audience
questions.explanation: Business journalism should translate specialist concepts without oversimplifying or distorting them.

questions.question: Which challenge is especially important in health reporting?
options: Avoiding all expert sources
Treating correlation as proof of causation
Promoting untested treatments as established cures
Communicating medical evidence accurately without causing unnecessary alarm
questions.explanation: Health stories can affect public behaviour, so reporters must explain evidence, uncertainty, risks, and limitations responsibly.

questions.question: What most clearly distinguishes feature writing from hard news?
options: Feature writing contains no facts
Hard news never uses quotations
Feature writing allows greater narrative depth, description, and creative structure
Features must always cover events occurring that day
questions.explanation: Features explore subjects more deeply and often use storytelling techniques, while hard news prioritises urgent facts.

questions.question: Which structure is most typical of hard news?
options: A fictional three-act structure
A diary arranged only by emotion
A bibliography-first structure
The inverted pyramid
questions.explanation: Hard news normally presents the most important information first for speed and clarity.

questions.question: Why may a feature writer use descriptive language?
options: To replace factual accuracy
To make the source impossible to identify
To create vivid scenes and deepen audience engagement
To turn every report into an advertisement
questions.explanation: Description can help readers visualise people, places, and experiences, but it must remain truthful.

questions.question: Why must beat reporters maintain objectivity despite their expertise?
options: Expertise permits them to omit opposing evidence
Long-term contacts must control the final story
Knowledge should improve accuracy, not turn reporting into advocacy for preferred sources
Objectivity applies only to general reporters
questions.explanation: Specialisation creates close relationships, so reporters must guard against capture, favouritism, and conflicts of interest.

questions.question: Why does broadcast writing favour short, conversational sentences?
options: Audiences usually hear the information once and must understand it immediately
Broadcast audiences read footnotes during transmission
Long sentences improve audio quality
Conversational language prevents all errors
questions.explanation: Broadcast copy is written for the ear, so clarity, brevity, and natural phrasing are essential.

questions.question: How does magazine writing commonly differ from straight newspaper news?
options: It never uses research
It often permits more depth, creativity, description, and visual presentation
It must always be shorter than a news brief
It cannot include quotations
questions.explanation: Magazine articles often provide extended analysis and storytelling supported by strong visuals.

questions.question: What makes online content scannable?
options: Dense blocks of text with no breaks
Long introductions that delay the main point
Removing all headings and links
Subheadings, short paragraphs, bullet points, and highlighted key information
questions.explanation: Online readers often scan, so visual structure helps them locate important information quickly.

questions.question: What is the best use of a hyperlink in an online news article?
options: To provide relevant evidence or additional context without overcrowding the main text
To send readers to unrelated advertising
To replace all source verification
To hide the origin of a quotation
questions.explanation: Useful links deepen understanding and show supporting sources while preserving readability.

questions.question: Why should social-media news posts be tailored to the platform?
options: Platforms differ in audience behaviour, length, visual style, and interaction features
Every platform requires identical wording
Only print audiences care about accuracy
Platform adaptation means changing the facts
questions.explanation: The same verified story may need different formats for X, Facebook, Instagram, or other platforms.

questions.question: What should remain unchanged when adapting one story for print, broadcast, and digital platforms?
options: The length of every sentence
The verified core facts
The number of hyperlinks
The visual layout
questions.explanation: Format and style may change by medium, but factual accuracy and meaning must remain consistent.

questions.question: What is defamation?
options: A false statement communicated to others that harms a person’s reputation
Any criticism of a public policy
A verified fact that someone dislikes
A private thought never communicated
questions.explanation: Defamation law protects reputation from false and damaging published or spoken claims.

questions.question: What is the difference between libel and slander?
options: Libel is written or recorded defamation, while slander is spoken defamation
Libel is always true, while slander is always false
Libel concerns government, while slander concerns business
Libel is ethical, while slander is legal
questions.explanation: The distinction is based mainly on the form in which the defamatory statement is communicated.

questions.question: When may public interest outweigh an individual’s privacy?
options: Whenever the story might attract many clicks
When disclosure reveals information of genuine importance to public welfare or accountability
Whenever a source offers private photographs
Whenever the person is unknown
questions.explanation: Public interest requires a legitimate societal benefit, not mere curiosity or commercial appeal.

questions.question: What is a conflict of interest in journalism?
options: A disagreement between two quoted sources
A story containing more than one viewpoint
A personal or financial interest that could improperly influence professional judgement
A deadline shared by several reporters
questions.explanation: Conflicts can undermine independence or create the appearance that coverage is biased.

questions.question: How should a journalist handle a significant personal conflict of interest?
options: Hide it from everyone
Disclose it to the editor and withdraw or apply safeguards where necessary
Accept gifts and promise favourable coverage
Remove all opposing evidence from the story
questions.explanation: Disclosure and appropriate reassignment or safeguards protect editorial independence and public trust.

questions.question: What is contempt of court in a reporting context?
options: Criticising a completed court judgment
Publishing material that improperly interferes with the administration of justice
Reporting the public location of a courthouse
Explaining the meaning of a legal term
questions.explanation: Reports that prejudice active proceedings or disobey court restrictions may amount to contempt.

questions.question: What does incitement involve?
options: A balanced debate about public policy
A report quoting verified election results
A correction of an earlier mistake
Communication that encourages imminent unlawful violence or harmful action
questions.explanation: Freedom of expression has legal limits, including direct encouragement of imminent violence.

questions.question: What is the main purpose of self-editing?
options: To avoid checking facts
To improve clarity, accuracy, coherence, and style before formal editorial review
To add unsupported claims
To prevent anyone else from reviewing the story
questions.explanation: Self-editing allows the writer to detect weaknesses and refine the draft before submission.

questions.question: Why can taking a short break before editing improve the process?
options: It guarantees every source changes their statement
It removes the need for proofreading
It helps the writer return with a fresher and more critical perspective
It automatically shortens the article
questions.explanation: Distance from the draft makes errors, repetition, and unclear passages easier to notice.

questions.question: Why is reading a draft aloud useful?
options: It verifies every statistic automatically
It replaces source checking
It makes legal review unnecessary
It reveals awkward phrasing, missing words, and problems with rhythm
questions.explanation: Hearing the text often exposes problems that silent reading misses.

questions.question: What is collaborative editing?
options: Several people work together to review and improve a story
One reporter publishes without review
Sources rewrite the story to favour themselves
An algorithm selects only the headline
questions.explanation: Collaboration draws on multiple perspectives to improve accuracy, clarity, structure, and consistency.

questions.question: What is the purpose of a final read-through by a senior editor?
options: To introduce new unverified allegations
To ensure the polished story meets factual, ethical, legal, and house-style standards
To remove every quotation
To change the central facts for dramatic effect
questions.explanation: The final review checks readiness for publication after revisions and corrections have been made.

questions.question: What is search engine optimisation in digital journalism?
options: Paying sources to share the story
Repeating one keyword in every sentence
Changing facts to match popular searches
The ethical use of structure, keywords, links, and metadata to improve an article’s discoverability
questions.explanation: SEO helps search engines understand and surface relevant articles without sacrificing quality or accuracy.

questions.question: What is keyword stuffing?
options: Adding a clear descriptive headline
Excessive and unnatural repetition of search terms to manipulate ranking
Linking to an official source
Writing a concise meta description
questions.explanation: Keyword stuffing damages readability and is a poor SEO practice; keywords should be used naturally.

questions.question: How can artificial intelligence assist a newsroom?
options: It guarantees that all generated content is correct
It eliminates ethical responsibility from editors
It can automate routine reports or support tasks such as transcription and fact-checking
It makes human verification unnecessary
questions.explanation: AI can improve efficiency, but journalists must verify outputs and remain accountable for published content.

questions.question: What is data journalism?
options: Using datasets and analysis to discover, verify, and explain news stories
Publishing numbers without interpretation
Replacing all interviews with advertising data
Writing fiction about statistics
questions.explanation: Data journalism finds patterns and evidence in data, then presents them accurately and clearly to audiences.

questions.question: What is multi-platform publishing?
options: Publishing one story in only one place
Allowing algorithms to change verified facts
Distributing adapted versions of news through websites, apps, social media, newsletters, print, or broadcast
Using the same layout on every device
questions.explanation: A multi-platform approach expands reach while requiring format-specific presentation and consistent facts.

questions.question: How do social-media algorithms affect news distribution?
options: They verify every claim before it appears
They guarantee equal visibility for all stories
They prevent audience personalisation
They influence which stories users see based partly on engagement and platform rules
questions.explanation: Algorithms shape visibility and can reward engagement, affecting how outlets package and promote stories.

questions.question: What is news personalisation?
options: Tailoring the news shown to users according to preferences or behaviour
Randomly removing every local report
Printing the same front page for everyone
Blocking all stories that contain data
questions.explanation: Personalisation can increase relevance but may also narrow exposure to diverse viewpoints.

questions.question: How can virtual or augmented reality contribute to journalism?
options: By replacing verification with simulation
By creating immersive experiences that help audiences explore a reported environment or event
By converting every story into a game
By preventing audiences from viewing evidence
